### 2026-10-18 – # Valkarye V3 - Devlog

# Valkarye V3 - Devlog

## First 15 Hours

A few years ago I built a robotic arm just as a small side project for fun. I ended up losing it over time, but I always wanted to come back and rebuild it properly. That is how Valkarye V3 started.

The old version was pretty basic and could barely hold its own weight. For V3, I want it to actually be useful. It needs to pick up and move real objects, respond to voice commands, and let me control every joint smoothly using an app on my phone or laptop.

Here is the log and engineering sketches for each of the first 15 hours.

---

### Hour 01: Teardown of the old arm and finding failure points

I spent the first hour thinking through what went wrong with the old robotic arm. The main issues were joint flex, stripped plastic gears, USB brownouts rebooting the board, and a wobbly base because there was no thrust bearing.

![Hour 01 Sketch]

![hour_01_old_arm_problems](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/179c861861e496685dde07e3a794d36f0d0368655f52b446050274928aae397a.png)

---

### Hour 02: Defining the Valkarye V3 concept and features

I mapped out what V3 needs to do differently. It needs 6 axes of movement, a dedicated phone and desktop web app for control over Wi-Fi, low latency WebSockets, and voice command parsing.

![Hour 02 Sketch]

![hour_02_valkarye_v3_concept](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/45dfa33eb204976961fe4bc06ea6fb43cbda4db662315742dc46056fa1c87166.png)

---

### Hour 03: System block diagram and interfaces

Layed out the hardware and communication architecture. The client app talks to an ESP32 over Wi-Fi, the ESP32 sends joint angles over I2C to a PCA9685 driver, and the PCA9685 drives the 6 servos. Added an external 5V 5A buck converter with a common ground rail.

![Hour 03 Sketch]

![hour_03_system_architecture](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/13af5764cdf752485e338269a4ad4e15a076901be25527c2f3e8dce11d555645.png)
---

### Hour 04: Mechanical joint layout and degrees of freedom

Planned the 6 degrees of freedom: Base yaw, Shoulder pitch, Elbow pitch, Wrist pitch, Wrist roll, and a Gripper claw. Assigned responsibilities to each joint to make sure the arm has full spherical reach.

![Hour 04 Sketch]

![hour_04_six_axis_dof](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/262a6ae4835d482bacf8cab364a120b50dad95d5b61f3620c621185784571c6b.png)

---

### Hour 05: Shoulder and elbow torque math

Did the torque calculations for worst-case arm extension with a 250g payload at 27cm reach. The shoulder needs at least 11.3 kg-cm of torque, which means plastic servos will never work here.

![Hour 05 Sketch]

![hour_05_torque_calculations](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/ce6f29e0f1b5dd35401379f10d8709fc72d1793c88f3ab0ff099bbf44760b676.png)
---

### Hour 06: Servo motor selection and weight tradeoffs

Decided on heavy-duty metal gear servos (MG996R / DS3218) for the base, shoulder, and elbow where torque is critical. For the wrist and claw, I chose lightweight MG90S micro servos to save weight at the tip of the arm.

![Hour 06 Sketch]

![hour_06_servo_selection](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/e31f1c19f3d99d77e3432a85bd3c36e8783cf88a69786ba474c796e09c5e6298.png)

---

### Hour 07: Power distribution circuit and buck converter

Designed the power delivery system. A 12V 5A wall power supply feeds an adjustable high-current buck converter stepped down to 5.2V for the servos, with a 1000uF capacitor to absorb motor surge currents so the ESP32 does not brown out.

![Hour 07 Sketch]

![hour_07_power_distribution](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/eff31b2f52db1e4664daa32bcc6e8d738b103fef9e85ac78d7bf0346a5dde1de.png)
---

### Hour 08: Wiring layout and I2C pin mapping

Mapped out the exact wiring connections between the ESP32 and PCA9685 board. GPIO 21 for SDA, GPIO 22 for SCL, logic power from 3.3V, and channels 0 through 5 mapped to the arm joints.

![Hour 08 Sketch]

![hour_08_i2c_pca9685_wiring](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/d7a0f81b762b4057fab1998dcc4926e20f0f8c52ffeda48fe54258976cdb3e87.png)
---

### Hour 09: Wireless communication and WebSockets pipeline

Designed the wireless link between the companion app and the ESP32. Chose WebSockets for two-way communication at 50Hz, giving real-time control with under 20ms of latency and live angle feedback.

![Hour 09 Sketch]

![hour_09_wireless_pipeline](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/a4bac93505267a48773861c89e9c8b034a6de9de7a88c4cf64287aa2968fcaa7.png)

---

### Hour 10: Packet structure and protocol definition

Wrote down the JSON packet format for joint angle commands, movement speed limits, and returning telemetry like current angles and supply voltage.

![Hour 10 Sketch]

![hour_10_packet_structure](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/a767ffb54fbadbca211a1af0f0c275d2b8a3b0d4c9a9686fa96910939478a6b8.png)

---

### Hour 11: Voice recognition and intent parser architecture

Designed the voice control pipeline. The voice capture and speech-to-text will run directly inside the companion app using the Web Speech API. The app parses the intent and calculates target coordinates before sending lightweight angle packets to the ESP32.

![Hour 11 Sketch]

![hour_11_voice_control_flow](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/bce9a9c2ce9eb1659bebad096c7083b3ea8f23fb55d6c2480bf77ec16b9be0ea.png)

---

### Hour 12: Software limits and safety endstops

Defined the safe angular envelope for every joint. Set software limits for base rotation, shoulder elevation, elbow flexion, and claw pinch so the arm cannot crash into itself or hit the table.

![Hour 12 Sketch]

![hour_12_software_limits](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/be07dd1aeab9cadf591ad1af348527f40766e13a23c04ce4e51e8be2fee1cd49.png)

---

### Hour 13: Kinematic workspace and arm reach geometry

Calculated the physical link lengths: 140mm for the bicep and 130mm for the forearm. This gives a total maximum reach of 330mm with an optimal pickup zone between 150mm and 250mm from the base.

![Hour 13 Sketch]

![hour_13_kinematics_workspace](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/c5462b14820a5b312ad32a5223182b5a1d0d7be31fa48e8e3162b4cf1835c29c.png)

---

### Hour 14: Base turntable and thrust bearing design

Designed the base turntable to solve the wobble issue from the old arm. Placed a 51105 thrust ball bearing between the rotating arm plate and the stationary base so all vertical weight rests on the bearing instead of the servo shaft.

![Hour 14 Sketch]

![hour_14_base_turntable](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/fc17a7fc055a5e1d59a9dea4b8e04db8caffb2c5a2fc080604f18bf1501c7762.png)

---

### Hour 15: Gripper mechanism and bill of materials

Sketched a parallel jaw gripper mechanism with silicone rubber pads driven by an MG90S micro servo, and finalized the complete bill of materials needed for Sprint 2.

![Hour 15 Sketch]

![hour_15_gripper_and_bom](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/hackclub-half-life/sessions/hekUGdMUsJvkfZr4IeTGwJeZETfm9ZrV/6941bf5d0c7497af89e1b56bbf868d5b8f602f6e8e80c66948338539faf8ad20.png)

---

### Summary of First 15 Hours

Total time logged: 15 hours.

All 15 hours of planning, system architecture, torque math, wireless protocol design, and mechanical sketches are complete. Next phase is 3D CAD modeling the joint brackets and running initial firmware tests on the bench.
